title: Showing, Hiding, and Toggling Elements
subtopics: Understanding interactions with CSS display rules
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of showing, hiding, and toggling elements in a jQuery application.
Apply .show() in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify .hide() with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through showing, hiding, and toggling elements with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns .show() into a repeatable implementation choice. jQuery can read dimensions, positioning, scroll offsets, and computed CSS. Prefer classes and responsive CSS for presentation state, and avoid mixing layout reads with repeated writes.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates showing, hiding, and toggling elements using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in showing, hiding, and toggling elements.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: Toggles a semantic CSS state class. Define .is-hidden in CSS and keep accessibility state synchronized where needed.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
summary: Showing, Hiding, and Toggling Elements is one part of the css, dimensions, and element positioning workflow.
jQuery can read dimensions, positioning, scroll offsets, and computed CSS. Prefer classes and responsive CSS for presentation state, and avoid mixing layout reads with repeated writes.
